preamble: Under Grimm's law the Proto-Indo-European voiced aspirate *gʰ (with palatovelar *ǵʰ, merged with it in Germanic) became Proto-Germanic /ɣ/. It was realized as the fricative [ɣ] between vowels and, in most reconstructions, word-initially, and as the stop [ɡ] after nasals and in gemination. The fricative survives in Dutch and Low German g. Outside Germanic the aspirate usually deaspirated (Balto-Slavic, Celtic, Iranian g) or devoiced (Greek kʰ, Italic h), so the direct change to [ɣ] is a Germanic feature.

examples.note: Gothic steigan, Old English stīgan, Dutch stijgen with [ɣ].
Old English wegan, English weigh, Dutch wegen.
Gothic daigs, Dutch deeg, German Teig.
Word-initial position; Old Norse gestr, Old English ġiest.

sources: Ringe, D. (2006). A History of English, Volume I: From Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199284139.001.0001
